doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Impressions of Cannonball Adderley
summary: He admires Cannonball's intelligence and humility, and tells how Cannonball went off for a lesson with Marshall Royal.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Let me run a couple of names by you and just get your impression of these musicians. One is Cannonball Adderley.

Tremendous respect. Loved him. Tremendous talent. Great, great musician. Great, great man. And you know the thing I learned from him? Somebody asked him once, said, “Mr. Adderley,” they said, “do you consider yourself a great or big man?” And Cannonball said to him, “Well a big man is judged by someone other than one’s self.” Hey, Hello? I mean a lot of people could say the same thing. Hello? See that’s another Virgo. I have tremendous respect for Cannonball Adderley, and his brother. You see what I’m saying. As a musician and as a human being. Well articulated you know. I heard him talking about something, “Ladies and Gentlemen we have this composition here written by James Heath, you know him as Jimmy Heath, and it’s called ‘Gemini’ and we’re going to pursue to endeavor all the parts.” I said, “Go ahead, Cannon.” He said, “We just got an article in this newspaper called All About Jazz” — and he’s talking about, Cannonball was an intelligent man, I mean he was smart man. Plus he made Coltrane good. You listen to those records, Cannonball didn’t back up for nobody. And he was studying. One day Jimmy Anessis said he saw Cannon, he said, “Hey Cannon” he said, “I’m sorry man I gotta run, I got a saxophone lesson.” He was going to take a lesson with Marshall Royal.
